12849-the-tinguian-social-religious-and-:
Fay-Cooper Cole's 1922 study, from the Field Museum, describes the Tinguian people of the northern Philippines in full detail. Chapters cover birth, childhood, marriage, death, religion, magic, ceremonies, village rule, warfare, hunting, and fishing, with rice culture, weaving, iron work, basketry, and pottery. Music and dance get their own sections.

Ceremonies anchor the account: a healing rite drives spirits from a village with spear and pole, while an oath rite tests thieves with rice wine. Cole writes as a careful field observer, not a romancer. The study remains a key source on a Philippine tribe before modern change.
14117-wanted-a-young-woman-to-do-housewo:
C. Hélène Barker's 1915 book argues that housework should run on the same fair terms as factory, shop, and office work. Part one diagnoses the trouble: ignorance in the home, scarce workers, and the low standing of domestic labor. Part two applies business rules: living outside the place of work, an eight-hour day, a six-day week, holidays kept, and extra pay for overtime.

Schedules make the reform concrete. Barker prints eight-hour plans for one, two, and three employees, and she counts hidden costs with care, from worn utensils and fuel to the labor of cooking and washing up for staff. Sickness and surprise guests receive frank treatment: extra hours deserve extra wages. Written before modern labor law reached the home, the book remains a clear, practical plea for dignity in domestic service.
25070-mr-opp:
Alice Hegan Rice's Mr. Opp, published by the Century Company in 1909, is a warm comic novel about a luckless man in a small river town. Mr. Opp has a talent for missing things: trains, jobs, patents, and chances of every kind, a habit his neighbors know well and tease him for.

When Opp sets up a printing press and starts a little newspaper, his fortunes begin to turn, though not without quarrels with sharp-tongued neighbors such as Mrs. Gusty and plenty of embarrassment along the way. Rice, beloved for Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch, writes with gentle humor and affection for ordinary people trying to make good.
25919-miss-mapp:
E. F. Benson sets a comedy of spying and spite in a small English town, with Miss Elizabeth Mapp at its center. Mapp, perhaps forty and glad to seem a year or two older, has a face of high color ridged by chronic rage and curiosity. Those very emotions keep her young and on the boil, and from her garden room window she watches the street that runs down to the High Street like a bird of prey.

The town buzzes with golf, duels that may not be duels, and gossip scraped like crab shells at tea. Diva argues no duel could fit with a full round of golf, since no nerves could stand both. Captain Puffin and the Major finish their match on the eighteenth hole while talk swirls. Benson writes of Tilling's wars of manners with wit sharp as Mapp's own tongue.
britannica-1911-abelin-johann-philipp:
Johann Philipp Abelin receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abelin, a German chronicler born likely at Strasburg, died there between 1634 and 1637. He wrote under names like Gottfried and Arlanibäus, compiling histories from records of his own day.

Arma Suecica told the German wars of Gustavus Adolphus in twelve parts, and the Inventarium Sueciae followed. His fame rests on the Theatrum Europaeum, a chronicle of world events to 1619 that grew to twenty-one volumes under later hands. Merian's copperplate engravings give the set its lasting beauty, the entry holds. A history of the antipodes and one of India came after his death. Droysen's study of his tangled pen names closes the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-onno-klopp:
German historian Onno Klopp, born at Leer in 1822, wrote for schools, courts, and kings across a long career. After reading philology and theology in Bonn, Berlin, and Göttingen and a Jena doctorate in 1845, he taught at Osnabrück until 1858 while publishing on school reform.

Klopp urged that language study begin with living tongues, not dead ones, and wrote popular histories of German tribes, emperors, and Admiral de Ruyter. Later court historian to the exiled Hanoverian king, he defended legitimist causes in massive works and died at Vienna in 1903. He taught at Osnabruck until 1858 while publishing on pedagogy and German history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sebastian-kne:
Sebastian Kneipp, Bavarian priest and hydrotherapist, was born at Stephansried on 17 May 1821 and died at Wörishofen on 17 June 1897. A poor weaver's son, he worked his father's trade as a journeyman while cherishing hopes of priesthood and spending spare hours in study. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a sick student who became a water-cure apostle.

A friendly priest helped him into the gymnasium, but five years of hard study and privation broke his health, and Kneipp developed consumption. Hearing of hydrotherapy's value, he tried it on himself, bathing briefly in the Danube two or three times a week in the winter of 1849 at Dillingen, then hurrying home. He reported no harm and, as he thought, small benefit, yet his health improved enough for Munich's Georgianum seminary, where he pressed on with water cures.

frus-1877app:
This appendix to the 1877 papers is a trade dossier. Two circulars from Washington set its task. Evarts asks officers in Spanish America for commercial reports. Seward sends the same call to Europe. Consuls must find markets for American goods. They must report which trades Americans can enter. The replies fill the volume country by country.

Argentina's press reaction opens the returns. An Austrian report blames American patent law for weak competition. Trieste's consul urges direct steam links and a sample warehouse. A German report describes mower and reaper markets flooded. English and imitation machines crowd the same fields. Agents matter more than machines, it concludes. The appendix is economic intelligence in raw form. It shows a trading nation studying its rivals.
frus-1914Supp:
The 1914 supplement is the war's first documentary history. Pre-war papers print the peace treaty campaign. Cooling-off treaties were Lansing's era's hope before the guns. Part I then follows the outbreak day by day. America's first mediation suggestion came on July 28. Good offices follow in early August. Turkey enters the war by November. Britain declares its protectorate over Egypt.

The Far East war gets its own block. Japan moves against Germany in China and the Pacific. Part II turns to neutral rights. Contraband lists and trade bans fill its pages. Copper shipments draw a special file. A mid-volume telegram reports German cruisers sinking English ships. Washington warns its Berlin ambassador that October. The supplement is chronology as diplomacy.
frus-1915Supp:
The 1915 supplement tracks the war's spread and the blockade's law. Part I follows new belligerents and peace feelers. Italy enters the war in its pages. Bulgaria follows, and the Allies intervene in Greece. Conditions inside Russia and the Central Empires are reported. Private peace efforts run beside official ones. Part II turns to neutral rights in earnest.

Germany declares a naval war zone in February 1915. Washington answers with proposals that same month. It would restrict mines, submarines, and false flags. Food supplies for Germany form part of the bargain. Britain and France then ban all trade with Germany. American protests against their orders fill the file. The supplement is the blockade argued in notes. Submarines and hunger drive its law.
frus-1916Supp:
The 1916 supplement follows the war's spread and the peace feelers. Portugal enters the war in March. Roumania follows in August, and Italy declares war on Germany. Spain proposes joint good offices in May. The belligerents reject that plan by August. Germany asks American help in September. Wilson hints in November that sinkings and deportations must stop. The Central Powers invite peace talks on December 12.

Wilson answers with his own suggestion days later. The mid-volume papers show the blockade's daily friction. A British firm, Herskovits and Company, is named undesirable. London will not say if trading with it breaks law. Such cases fill the neutral rights files. The supplement ends with peace in the air. Submarines decide whether it lands.
frus-1955-57v03mSupp:
A microfiche supplement to the China volume stands here as its own record. It gathers the full run of reports on the Geneva ambassadorial talks. Ambassador Johnson's accounts, his comments, and his orders from Washington fill the files.

Meetings are listed from August 1, 1955, through December 12, 1957. The print volume took a selection; this set takes all of it. Some pages are flawed, and the editors mark gaps where the film failed. Scholars use the supplement to check each claim made at the table against the orders behind it. The fiche order holds the China files apart from the wider Asia set.
frus-1958-60v03mSupp:
The microfiche supplement to Volume III of the 1958–1960 set adds hundreds of papers on security policy and arms control. National security policy runs first, in Documents 1–286. Arms control and disarmament follow, in Documents 287–608.

The digital text keeps the fiche order, with editors' notes on missing or blurred pages. A mid-sample estimate weighs a Soviet pressure campaign. The files deepen the print volume's record. Staff drafts, side memos, and annexes that print left out appear here in full, gaps and all, for the close reader. Many pages carry the stamps and gaps of the fiche itself.
frus-1958-60v05mSupp:
The microfiche supplement to Volume V of the 1958–1960 set holds the country files print left out. Regional aid policy leads. Then Bolivia through Venezuela run in country blocks, each with its own code.

Panama takes the longest run, on canal and flag questions. El Salvador's files end with the 1960 junta's bid for recognition. The digital text keeps the fiche order. Papers blurred or stamped best copy available appear as found. The supplement turns a thin print record into a full one for most of the hemisphere. Country codes mark each block for the fiche reader.
frus-1961-63v07-09mSupp:

Security policy follows, Documents 226–310. Economic policy closes the set, by topic and month. A mid-sample paper urges a free-world web of ties among firms, unions, and churches. The digital text keeps the fiche order. Print volumes hold the peaks; this supplement holds the staff work under them, month by month. The fiche order runs month by month throughout.
frus-1961-63v10-12mSupp:

Country papers for the hemisphere follow, capital by capital. The digital text keeps the fiche order, with editors' notes on gaps and blurred pages. Print holds the summits and the crisis calls. govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FieldCapp_Field:
Six days after the assassination, the FBI recorded a lead about photographs. A memorandum dated November 28, 1963 states that Eddie Barker of KRLD reported that a man named Capp Field possessed photographs of the assassination. In those first days, every camera in Dealey Plaza mattered to investigators.

Amateur film and photographs became core evidence in the Kennedy case, because they fixed the shooting in frames. A report that one more man held pictures sent agents to find him. The memo preserves that lead as the Bureau logged it, part of the great gathering of images from Dallas.
nasa-tm-19690017325-cowell-type-numerica:
Jesse L. Maury Jr. and Gail P. Segal of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this April 1969 preprint, X-553-69-46. They apply Cowell-type numerical integration to satellite orbit computation. Cowell's approach steps an orbit forward by summing every force acting on the satellite. Orbit equations have no exact written solution, so computers must build the path step by step.

The opening chapters weigh one-step methods against multistep methods for such problems. One-step methods need only the last computed point, but they err more and cost more evaluations. Multistep methods reuse several past points and reach high accuracy with larger steps. High speed computers, the authors note, made this precision practical at all. Their study puts the multistep Cowell approach to work on real satellite orbits.
the-tinguian-social-religious-and-econom: Fay-Cooper Cole, assistant curator of Malayan ethnology, published The Tinguian in 1922. It studies the social, religious, and economic life of a Philippine tribe. This record gives his title page and a full contents list, not the study's text. The contents run from geography and physical type through the cycle of life, birth to burial. Then come religion and magic, the great ceremonies, and social organization. Rice culture and industries such as iron-working and weaving close the list. Cole's fieldwork is mapped, though his findings begin past these leaves.
wanted-a-young-woman-to-do-housework-bus: C. Helene Barker wrote Wanted, a Young Woman to Do Housework, on business principles applied to housework. Moffat, Yard and Company issued it at New York in 1915. Pages present here hold the title page and the contents, so her argument itself is not shown. The contents lay out a plan in three parts. First come the causes of the present poor state of domestic labor. Servants would live out, work an eight-hour day and a six-day week, and gain extra pay for overtime.
